title: Rewinding the Universe
question: How do we know the universe began hot and dense?
hook: Run the expansion backward and everything squeezes together.
idea: Expansion, leftover radiation and the first elements all point back to a hot, dense start.

beats.prompt: Astronomers extrapolate the universe's expansion backward in time using the known laws of physics. What do the models describe?

choices.label: An extraordinarily hot and dense primordial universe
A cold, empty universe much like today
choices.feedback: Running expansion backward packs things closer together, which makes them hotter, not emptier.

choices.label: A universe of the same size and density as now
choices.feedback: The universe is expanding, so earlier it was smaller and denser.

beats.explain: Extrapolating the expansion backward describes an extraordinarily hot and dense primordial universe.

items: Hubble publishes the work known as Hubble's law
The CMB is discovered by accident
beats.explain: Friedmann's idea came in 1922, Hubble's law in 1929, Lemaître's proposal in 1931 and the CMB in 1964.

beats.prompt: Match each idea to its role in Big Bang models.
pairs: Turned inflation's energy into hot plasma
Aided gravity in forming early stars and galaxies
beats.explain: Each idea plays a different part in the story from the earliest stages to today.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: The universe has a finite age.
Light travels at a finite speed.
So light from every past event has already reached us.
So there is no limit on the most distant objects we can observe.
beats.explain: With a finite age and finite light speed, some past events may not have had time to send light to Earth, which sets a limit.
